ecolongr: design

Source: DESIGN.md

Problem

vegan needs the full taxa × samples matrix in memory, dense. For amplicon data with millions of ASVs and thousands of samples this is tens of gigabytes, although almost all cells are zero. Selecting rows and columns first helps, but does not remove the problem.

Related: asvoccur#1 proposes keeping occurrence data as a long table (Parquet/DuckDB). This package would compute the common vegan analyses directly from such a table.

Goal

Re-implement a small subset of vegan, taking a long table as input, with results that agree with vegan to numerical tolerance. vegan is the reference implementation and the test oracle.

Non-goals

  • Replacing vegan. Anything that only needs a distance matrix is left to vegan.
  • Constrained ordination (rda with explanatory variables), for now. See “rda with explanatory variables: postponed”.
  • Plotting, including ggplot2 interfaces. Result objects keep the vegan classes, so existing tools that plot vegan objects (ggvegan, ggordiplots, microViz) should work on them. Which of these are maintained and cover rda and dist has not been checked.

Where the memory goes

The taxa axis is the large one. After a sample × sample distance exists, that axis is gone. So methods split by whether they need the taxa × samples matrix:

vegan method Needs the matrix? In ecolongr
vegdist yes el_vegdist(), a compiled kernel over a table sorted by taxon
rarefy, drarefy no, one sample at a time el_rarefy(), el_drarefy(), lazy apart from the distinct (total, count) pairs
rrarefy no, one sample at a time el_rrarefy(), materializes the input; drawn in C++
diversity, specnumber no, one sample at a time el_diversity(), el_specnumber(), lazy grouped sums in DuckDB; only one number per sample is read into R; 10.9M rows add 37 MB with 4 threads (see diversity and specnumber)
decostand yes el_decostand() for the methods that need only non-zero cells; clr and the completed rclr are computed inside el_vegdist() and el_rda()
rda, unconstrained (PCA) yes el_rda(), truncated SVD of an implicitly centred sparse matrix
metaMDS no, takes a dist vegan on our dist
adonis2 no, takes a dist vegan on our dist
dbrda, capscale no, take a dist vegan on our dist
envfit no, takes an ordination vegan on an el_rda() or metaMDS() result

metaMDS wraps monoMDS, a nonmetric optimiser with random starts and local minima, so a re-implementation would only agree approximately. adonis2 makes an n × n copy internally, which only matters at very large n. Both can be revisited if profiling says otherwise.

Input

The input is a long table with columns sample, taxon and quant, as a data frame or a lazy duckplyr table. A sparse matrix is not accepted; the README shows how to turn a dgCMatrix into a long table with Matrix::summary().

A sparse matrix is the natural in-memory format for the linear algebra (irlba, C++ kernels). The problem to avoid is the dense conversion, not the sparse matrix. The flow is therefore: query the long table, select, build a sparse matrix only where an algorithm needs one (el_rda() and the matrix completion).

Data sources

  • nf-core/ampliseq 3.0.0 and later write summary_tables/ampliseq.counts.parquet: a long table with columns asv_id, sample and count, zero rows dropped. It is DADA2 output before clustering and filtering, so it exists only with --asv_calling dada2.
  • The same directory has one taxonomy table per classifier and database, keyed by asv_id, with flag columns such as ampliseq_accept. Join on asv_id to select ASVs, for example only those that passed all filters.
  • asvoccur (see above) is the other source: public SBDI data, with eventID and taxonID in place of sample and asv_id.

Both give a long table with a sample, a taxon and a count, which is the input contract below. A small subset of the ampliseq tables is a candidate test fixture beside the vegan data sets.

duckplyr interface

Users filter, join and reshape with duckplyr verbs, then pass the unevaluated table to ecolongr. Each function keeps working lazily for as long as the operation allows, and materializes only where it must.

Contract

  • Input: a lazy table (duckplyr_df or duckdb_tibble) with a sample, a taxon and a quantity column, by default sample, taxon and quant. The column names are arguments. The quantity is called quant and not count, because it may be a relative abundance or a transformed value. A plain data frame is converted on entry.
  • samples (optional): a lazy table or vector of sample IDs defining the full set of samples. A long table without zeros cannot show a sample whose counts are all zero, so such a sample is silently absent unless samples lists it. Without samples, the sample set is the samples that occur in the table, and the documentation says so. In asvoccur the events table is the natural source.
  • decostand: lazy in, lazy out, as a long table.
  • vegdist: the lazy query is run by DuckDB and written to a temporary Parquet file. A compiled kernel reads it in batches of whole taxa and adds up the pairs. The result is a dist, which is n × n and so materialized by definition.
  • rda (PCA): pulls only the non-zero triplets into R to build the sparse matrix for irlba. The size is the number of non-zero cells, not taxa × samples.
  • Each function documents where it materializes.

Example

library(duckplyr)
library(ecolongr)

counts <- read_parquet_duckdb("summary_tables/ampliseq.counts.parquet")
taxonomy <- read_parquet_duckdb(
  "summary_tables/ampliseq.taxonomy.DADA2.consolidated_most-specific.parquet"
)

nmds <- counts |>
  semi_join(taxonomy, by = "asv_id") |>
  mutate(relab = count / sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .by = sample) |>
  transmute(taxon = asv_id, sample, quant = relab) |>
  el_vegdist(method = "bray") |>
  vegan::metaMDS()
  • The semi_join() keeps the ASVs that have a row in the taxonomy table. Taxonomy is assigned only after clustering and filtering, so this drops clustered-away and filtered ASVs from the counts. The file name is for --consolidate_taxonomies most-specific; with one database it is ampliseq.taxonomy.DADA2.<database>.parquet. A filter() on the taxonomy table, for example on domain, narrows the selection further before the join.
  • Everything before el_vegdist() is lazy. el_vegdist() runs the query and returns a dist; metaMDS() is plain vegan.
  • Use .by = for grouped work. group_by() is not translated by duckplyr: it falls back to dplyr and materializes.
  • Window functions need na.rm = TRUE: sum(count) inside mutate(.by = ) is not translated, sum(count, na.rm = TRUE) is. The same holds for mean(). The example above was checked on a stingy frame (see below) on 2026-10-10.
  • The example renames to the default column names with transmute().
  • ecolongr does not attach duckplyr. Attaching duckplyr replaces dplyr verbs for data frames, which is a choice for the user’s session, not for a package.

Silent fallback

duckplyr falls back to dplyr without an error when it meets a verb it cannot translate, and the whole table is then materialized in R. The only sign is the duckplyr: materializing message, shown with options(duckdb.materialize_message = TRUE). For a package whose purpose is saving memory this must not happen unnoticed, so:

  • Every function needs a test that its pipeline stays lazy until the documented materialization point.
  • duckplyr has no switch that turns a fallback into an error; fallback_config() only controls logging and uploading, by design. The guard is the prudence of the frame. A frame made with as_duckdb_tibble(x, prudence = "stingy") raises “This operation cannot be carried out by DuckDB” on any verb that would fall back, and collect() or as.data.frame() on a query DuckDB can run still work.
  • Every function converts its input with prudence = "stingy", so an untranslatable verb inside ecolongr is an error, not a silent copy.
  • as_duckdb_tibble() on a frame that is already a duckplyr_df returns a lavish one, so the guard is applied by the function and does not depend on what the user passed.
  • Users can do the same in their own pipelines by making the first table stingy. ecolongr cannot see a fallback that happened before the table reached it.

Evidence so far

A scratch test on vegan::varespec as a long table:

  • semi_join, filter, a many-to-many self-join on taxon, grouped summarise, further joins and if_else inside summarise run on a stingy frame.
  • Bray–Curtis built from that pipeline matched vegan::vegdist to about 5e-16 over 66 sample pairs.
  • rclr as mutate(log(count) - mean(log(count), na.rm = TRUE), .by = sample) runs on a stingy frame. Without na.rm = TRUE it falls back. el_decostand("rclr") is tested against vegan::decostand(..., "rclr", impute = FALSE) on the non-zero cells.
  • mutate(relab = count / sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .by = sample) and transmute() run on a stingy frame; group_by() and sum(count) without na.rm do not.
  • mutate(z = rev(count), .by = sample) fell back to dplyr and materialized.

duckplyr translates few functions. Checked on 2026-10-10: log, log10, abs, round, as.integer, arithmetic and comparisons work; sqrt, exp, floor, ^, pmin, ifelse, cross_join and sum() without na.rm inside a window do not.

Cost

A many-to-many self-join on taxon produces, for each taxon, (number of samples containing it)² rows. On a skewed synthetic table (a few taxa in nearly every sample) this did not work as a DuckDB query:

samples pair operations DuckDB self-join compiled kernel (first version)
1,000 73M 7.8 s, 2.9 GB 0.7 s, 0.29 GB
2,000 343M killed at 14.6 GB after 30 min; 34 s and 4.3 GB with memory_limit 3.9 s, 0.39 GB

el_vegdist() therefore uses DuckDB only to select, sort and number the table, and a compiled kernel (src/kernel.cpp) to add up the pairs. The kernel adds into one vector of n(n−1)/2 numbers, in the order of a dist object, so no pair table is built. Samples are sorted within each taxon, blocks of sample ids are handled by one thread at a time, and the minima are computed in a vectorisable pass. The result is bit-identical for any number of threads.

Measured on 5,000 samples, 11.1M table rows and 10.5 billion pair operations (a shared 24-core machine under load):

version time peak memory
first kernel 478 s 1.8 GB
+ sorting within taxa 90 s 1.6 GB
+ branch-free minima, own DuckDB connection, integer ids (1 thread) 30 s 0.77 GB
same, 12 threads 7.2 s 1.0 GB

The peak is the dist (100 MB here), one batch, DuckDB’s memory_limit for the sort (default 250 MB, spills to disk), and the first step, which writes the lazy query to Parquet in the duckplyr connection (about 570 MB of buffers at 24 threads, which belongs to the user’s session and is left alone). Measured on 20,000 samples, 19.4M table rows and 60.5 billion pair operations: 25 s with 12 threads (148 s with one), peak 2.4 GB, of which the dist is 1.6 GB. A dense taxa × samples matrix for the same table (500,000 taxa) would be about 80 GB.

Against vegan::vegdist on a smaller skewed table that does fit in memory (2,000 samples, 50,000 taxa, 928k rows, Bray–Curtis, from bench/gen.R with exponent 1), on a laptop (Intel Core i5-1245U, 12 threads, 30 GB):

time peak memory
el_vegdist(), 4 threads 1.0 s 398 MB
vegan::vegdist() on the dense matrix (754 MB), 1 thread not finished after about 14 minutes 1.1 GB before it started

vegan::vegdist() was stopped by a 15-minute limit on the whole script, so the real ratio is larger than 800. Building the dense matrix from the long table is not counted in either time. The two results were not compared on this table; equality with vegan is covered by the tests on smaller tables. This is one skewed table and one metric, not a general speed-up.

Lazy steps before el_vegdist() run in the duckplyr connection of the user’s session, with DuckDB’s defaults (all cores, 80% of RAM). On the 5,000-sample table, el_decostand() followed by el_vegdist(method = "euclidean") took 11–12 s and peaked at 2.4 GB for total and rclr and 3.9 GB for log (a table-wide window). After duckplyr::db_exec("SET memory_limit = '500MB'") and duckplyr::db_exec("SET threads = 4") in the session, the same pipelines took 14–15 s and peaked at 1.1 GB. The package does not change these settings; the documentation should tell users on small machines to set them.

Memory grows with the square of the number of samples: 1.6 GB for 20,000 samples and 10 GB for 50,000.

Function names

Decision: the prefix el_, for example el_vegdist, el_decostand, el_rda.

  • The functions are not drop-in replacements: the input is a lazy long table, only a subset of the options exists, and rda returns the first k axes.
  • With the same names, library(vegan); library(ecolongr) masks vegdist, decostand and rda. Old scripts then fail confusingly, or silently call the wrong function.
  • vegan::vegdist is a plain function, not an S3 generic, so a method for our input class cannot coexist with it.
  • Writing ecolongr::vegdist() avoids the clash, but only if every example and user script does so.
  • A prefix lets both packages be attached, and shows in each call which one is meant. It also groups the functions in autocompletion.

Result objects keep the vegan classes (dist, and rda where feasible), so that vegan::metaMDS, vegan::adonis2, scores() and plot() work on them.

What is implemented

vegdist

  • Indices: bray, jaccard, euclidean, manhattan, canberra, aitchison and robust.aitchison (see decostand). Manhattan is Σx_i + Σx_j − 2 Σ min(x_i, x_j) and uses the same kernel as Bray–Curtis. Canberra follows vegan: terms where both samples are zero are dropped and the sum is divided by the number of taxa in either sample, so it is NA between two all-zero samples. It needs the number of shared taxa as well, which the kernel counts in the same pass.
  • Option: binary.
  • Bray–Curtis is 1 - 2·Σ min(x_i, x_j) / (Σ x_i + Σ x_j). Only taxa present in both samples contribute to the sum of minima. Cost is the sum over taxa of (samples containing the taxon)².
  • Returns a dist object, so the result can go straight into vegan::metaMDS, vegan::adonis2, hclust and so on.
  • Samples with zero total counts are only seen if listed in samples. Listed ones are treated as all-zero rows, as in vegan:
    • Bray–Curtis and Jaccard are NaN for a zero–zero pair, and 1 for a zero sample against a non-empty one.
    • Euclidean between a zero sample and another is the norm of the other.
    • Omitting such a sample changes the result, not only the dimensions of the dist.

rrarefy

Implemented as el_rrarefy(x, depth, sample, taxon, quant): a random subsample, without replacement, of depth individuals from each sample. Samples with a total at or below depth are returned unchanged, with a warning when below, as in vegan.

  • It materializes the input: the table is read into R and each sample is drawn in C++ (src/rarefy.cpp). The R side copies the table several times, so it needs a few times the memory of the input (a 412 MB table peaked at 1.3 GB). The result is a table with at most depth rows per sample.
  • Counts or sample totals of about 2^31 and above make R’s rhyper switch to a slow inversion, about 7 s for one sample at depth 5e8; the result is still correct.
  • vegan::rrarefy() draws the individuals one at a time (do_rrarefy in nestedness.c). el_rrarefy() draws the count of each taxon from the hypergeometric distribution of what is left, which costs one draw per taxon and not one per individual. Both give the multivariate hypergeometric distribution of counts, but not the same numbers for the same seed, so the result cannot be compared with vegan to 1e-10.
  • The tests instead draw 4,000 replicates of a small table and compare, per cell, the mean and the variance with vegan’s and with the exact hypergeometric values. The variance matters: sampling with replacement has the right mean and a variance too large by the finite population correction.
  • Not implemented: a depth per sample. Alpha diversity is el_diversity() and el_specnumber(); el_rarefy() gives expected richness at equal depth.

frequency_counts

Implemented as el_frequency_counts(x): for each sample, the number of taxa seen exactly k times, for each k present. It is one grouped count, so the table stays lazy and its size depends on the number of distinct counts, not on the number of taxa. There is no vegan function for it; the tests compare it with table() of each sample’s counts, and check that the frequencies add up to specnumber() and to the sample totals.

It is the input of richness estimators that count the unseen taxa (breakaway, Chao1, Chao-Bunge), which fit a model to this table in R. Those estimators are not implemented; see “Open questions”.

drarefy and rarefy

Implemented as el_drarefy(x, depth) and el_rarefy(x, depth): the expected presence of each taxon, and the expected richness of each sample, in a subsample of depth individuals. Deterministic, so the tests compare them with vegan::drarefy and vegan::rarefy at 1e-10 on BCI, the synthetic community and one sample of 2 million individuals. They are also compared with the mean over 4,000 el_rrarefy() replicates.

  • The probability that a taxon is present depends only on the sample total and the count. A lazy query finds the distinct pairs, R computes the probability for each with lchoose() as vegan does, and a join puts it back. el_drarefy() stays a lazy long table; el_rarefy() reads only the distinct (sample, total, count) combinations.
  • The first version computed it in DuckDB with lgamma(). The difference of two large lgamma values loses digits, and the result was off by 1e-9 at 1e5 individuals and 1e-6 at 1e7 with a small depth, against 1e-12 for vegan. DuckDB has no log1p, so the stable form could not be written in SQL.
  • Not implemented: se = TRUE, which needs a sum over pairs of taxa, and several depths at once (call the function once per depth). rarecurve() is not planned, since it is a plot.

diversity and specnumber

Implemented as el_diversity(x, index, base) and el_specnumber(x): one value per sample, as a numeric vector named by sample. The tests compare them with vegan::diversity() and vegan::specnumber() at 1e-10 on varespec (all 24 sites), the first 15 sites of BCI and the synthetic community, for all three indices, bases 2 and 10, and richness. Other tests cover a sample with one taxon, identical samples, proportions and a common scale, rows with quant == 0, duplicated rows, NaN and Inf, and the names of the result.

  • Lazy, and no window. The sample totals are a summarise(.by = sample), an inner_join() puts each total back on its rows, p = quant / total is a plain mutate(), and a second summarise(.by = sample) sums p * log(p) or p * p. The first version wrote quant / sum(quant, na.rm = TRUE) as a window in mutate(.by = sample), which DuckDB evaluates by buffering the whole table. p is formed before the sums on purpose: a sum of quant * quant overflows near 1e154, and log(S) - sum(x * log(x)) / S cancels. A peak-memory test fails for a window version (test-memory.R).

  • Measured on a table of 10.9M rows, 2,000 samples and 30,000 taxa (uniform), check = FALSE, an installed package, a fresh R process, extra peak memory over the process before the call:

    4 threads 12 threads
    el_diversity(), join version 37 MB, 0.3 s 217 MB, 0.2 s
    el_diversity(), window version 1,061 MB, 2.8 s 1,295 MB, 2.3 s
    el_specnumber() 21 MB 166 MB

    The three indices were within 2 MB of each other. With memory_limit = '500MB' in the session the join version added 29 MB and the window version 540 MB. The extra memory is DuckDB’s per-thread buffers, so it depends on the session’s threads, and not on the number of rows or taxa within what was measured. Only the 2,000 values are read into R. This is one synthetic uniform table; a skewed one was not measured.

  • Shannon is -sum(p * log(p)) / log(base). duckplyr translates log() but not a two-argument log(x, base), so the base is divided out in R on the per-sample result. Simpson is 1 - sum(p * p) and inverse Simpson 1 / sum(p * p), with p * p because ^ is not translated.

  • The sums are not compensated: with 1e7 equally common taxa in one sample the relative difference from vegan is about 2e-11 (measured by a reviewer), and the last digits can differ between runs with several threads.

  • Quantities need not be whole numbers. vegan divides by the sample total, so proportions, and any common scale, give the same result. Negative, missing and non-finite quantities are errors that name the column; check = FALSE skips the query that looks for them. A sample total above about 1e308 (the sum overflows) is not checked.

  • The non-finite check is quant > .Machine$double.xmax: DuckDB orders NaN and Inf above every finite number, is.nan() and is.finite() are not translated, and NaN is not NULL to DuckDB, so it was not caught by the missing check. check_quantities() is shared, so el_decostand(), el_drarefy() and el_rarefy() now reject NaN and Inf too.

  • Rows with quant == 0 are dropped. The table needs one row per sample and taxon, as everywhere in the package; rows are not merged, so a duplicated pair counts as two taxa.

  • All-zero samples: vegan gives an all-zero row Shannon 0, Simpson 1, inverse Simpson Inf and richness 0 (the 0/0 proportions are NaN and are dropped from the sums, which vegan::diversity() then reads as an empty sum). A long table cannot show such a sample, so it is absent from the result, and no entry is made up for it. The only difference from vegan is therefore the missing entries; the documentation lists the values to fill in. There is no samples argument here: a caller who has the full set of sample IDs can fill in the missing ones.

  • The names are the samples as character, sorted as text. Factor samples are not in level order, numeric samples sort as "10" < "9", an NA sample is named NA and comes last, and numbers that print the same as character share a name.

  • Not implemented: groups, MARGIN and equalize.groups of diversity(), and renyi(), fisher.alpha(), estimateR(), specpool() and evenness. Pielou’s evenness is el_diversity() / log(el_specnumber()), which the caller can compute.

decostand

Methods that act within a sample and need only the non-zero cells, so the result stays a long table without zeros. Implemented as el_decostand(); the result is a lazy duckplyr table and the tests compare every method with vegan::decostand.

  • total, log, pa, rclr: lazy queries.
  • hellinger: duckplyr cannot translate sqrt(), so the relative abundances are written to a temporary Parquet file and the square root is taken in SQL (read_sql_duckdb()). The file stays until the R session ends.
  • log follows vegan: log_b(x) + 1, and if any value in the whole table is not a whole number, all values are first divided by the smallest positive value of the table (a table-wide window, not per sample). There is no warning.
  • rclr: log(x / g(x > 0)), where g is the geometric mean of the positive values in the sample. vegan 2.7-6 returns NA for zeros with impute = FALSE, and the non-zero cells equal log(x) - mean(log(x[x > 0])) exactly. Called without impute, it fills the zeros by matrix completion, so the reference call must pass impute = FALSE. In a long table the zeros are simply absent rows.
  • el_decostand("rclr") leaves zeros absent, so a later step that reads absent cells as 0 puts those taxa at the sample’s geometric mean. That is not vegan’s robust Aitchison distance when zeros are present: vegdist(method = "robust.aitchison") is Euclidean distance on decostand(x, "rclr") with the default impute = TRUE (Martino et al. 2019). That step fills the missing cells by matrix completion of rank ropt (OptSpace, default rank 3, 5 iterations) and then centres rows and columns to mean 0, which also changes the non-zero cells. The two agree when the table has no zeros (tested). On the synthetic test table (80% zeros) they differ by up to 4.4 where the distances range up to 3.4.
  • The completed version is implemented as el_vegdist(method = "robust.aitchison") and el_rda(transform = "rclr"), both from raw counts. OptSpace runs on the observed cells only (the algorithm, constants and line search follow vegan::optspace(), and the result agrees to 1e-14), with Rcpp helpers for the sums over cells. The completed matrix has rank ropt: after centring it is Xc S Yc', so distances come from the ropt-column factors via a QR of Yc, and the PCA from an SVD of a ropt × ropt core. el_rda therefore returns at most ropt axes, scale = TRUE is not available, and samples with no non-zero cell are rejected (they have nothing to complete from).
  • ropt is an argument of el_vegdist() (for robust.aitchison) and el_rda() (for transform = "rclr"), named and defaulted (3) as in vegan, where decostand(x, "rclr", ropt = ) passes it to optspace(). It must be a whole number below the number of samples and of taxa, and giving it with any other method or transform is an error. Tested against vegan for ranks 2, 3 and 5. Speed and memory were measured only at rank 3: the cost of each OptSpace iteration grows with the rank, but how much on a large table is not measured. On the full LMO series (414 samples, 60,633 ASVs) it takes under two seconds, against 80 seconds for vegan’s dense completion, with the same seasonal R² (0.303). Measured on sequoia: 5,000 samples and 11.1M cells, robust.aitchison 38 s and 1.4 GB, el_rda 37 s and 1.7 GB; 20,000 samples and 19.4M cells, 87 s and 2.3 GB, and 72 s and 2.8 GB. The 20,000-sample run found an integer overflow in p * n (about 1e10), now fixed and covered by a test.
  • check = TRUE (default) runs one query to stop on negative or missing quantities; check = FALSE is fully lazy.

clr with a pseudocount has no long-table form, because it makes every cell non-zero. It is therefore not a method of el_decostand() (which stops and says so) but is computed from the raw counts inside el_vegdist(method = "aitchison") and el_rda(transform = "clr").

clr

  • A clr row is log(x + pc) minus its mean over the p taxa. Write b = log(1 + x / pc), which is 0 for a zero cell and sparse. The row mean of log(x + pc) is log(pc) plus the mean of b, so the clr row is b minus its row mean: a sparse matrix, centred per row.
  • Aitchison distance (Euclidean on clr) between samples i and j is sqrt(Σb_i² + Σb_j² − 2 Σ_shared b_i b_j − (Σb_i − Σb_j)² / p). The shared products are the same kernel as for Euclidean distance.
  • The centred clr matrix is B − u 1' − 1 c' with B sparse, so el_rda() uses an implicit operator for irlba, and the exact solver for small tables.
  • pseudocount is in the units of the counts: a positive number, "inverse_depth" for 1 / (the sample's total count), or a numeric vector named by sample. Give raw counts, not relative abundances. The user’s practice is count + 1/N_i per sample, which compensates for the higher detection limit of shallow samples.
  • The taxa of the table define p, as vegan after dropping all-zero columns. An all-zero sample listed in samples is the zero row of vegan: its clr is 0 and it sits at the origin.
  • Measured on sequoia: 5,000 samples and 11.1M rows, el_vegdist 11 s and 1.0 GB, el_rda (5 axes) 35 s and 1.7 GB; 20,000 samples and 19.4M rows, 29 s and 2.8 GB, and 62 s and 3.1 GB.
  • On the LMO time series (414 samples, 60,633 ASVs, 99% zeros), el_rda on the full table takes under a second and reproduces the dense vegan results exactly.

Choosing a transformation

On the LMO series, judged by how well PC1–PC2 show the seasonal cycle (see the memory notes of the analysis): Hellinger is good with or without filtering (seasonal R² 0.65), clr is poor on all 60,633 ASVs (0.28) but matches Hellinger once ASVs present in fewer than 20% of the samples are removed (0.64), and rclr with zeros as 0 is poor throughout (0.19–0.38). The pseudocount mattered little, smaller ones doing slightly better. clr should be used on a prevalence-filtered table.

rda, unconstrained

Implemented as el_rda().

  • Truncated SVD of the centred (and optionally scaled) matrix, with the centring applied implicitly so the matrix is never densified. Small tables use a dense SVD (solver = "exact"), larger ones irlba::irlba() on a sparse matrix built from the non-zero rows.
  • Total inertia is computed without densifying: Σ x² − n · mean² per column. This gives the proportion explained per axis.
  • n is the number of samples in the full set. All-zero samples listed in samples count in n, the column means and the total inertia, as zero rows do in vegan.
  • Only the first k axes are returned, where vegan returns all. The share of the total variance that they hold depends on k, so el_rda() reports it in a message after the fit, as metaMDS() reports its stress. options(ecolongr.quiet = TRUE) turns it off. The documentation says to divide an eigenvalue by tot.chi, not by the sum of the k eigenvalues, which sums to one and hides the rest.
  • The result has class ecolongr_rda, rda and cca, so scores() (scalings 1, 2 and 3), eigenvals(), summary(), plot(), biplot(), screeplot(), envfit() and procrustes() work (tested against vegan). predict() and fitted() need the full matrix and give an error. anova() gives vegan’s table for an unconstrained ordination, which has no constrained component.
  • The extra class exists for one eigenvals() method that sets the sumev attribute to the total inertia. Without it summary() takes the proportions of the k kept eigenvalues instead of the whole.
  • Axis signs are arbitrary.
  • Input is a transformed long table, composed with el_decostand(), or raw counts with transform = "clr" or "rclr". The clr fills the matrix, but only with one constant per sample, so it is a sparse matrix plus a rank-1 term and fits the implicit method.

Measured on sequoia, 5 axes, with 12 or fewer threads for the sort and irlba single-threaded:

table untransformed rclr
5,000 samples, 300,000 taxa, 11.1M rows 35 s, 1.4 GB 27 s, 3.0 GB
20,000 samples, 499,000 taxa, 19.4M rows 63 s, 2.2 GB 54 s, 3.8 GB

A dense matrix for the second table would be about 80 GB. The higher peak with rclr is the lazy window step in the duckplyr connection (see above).

rda with explanatory variables: postponed

vegan::rda(Y ~ X) takes a second, small matrix of explanatory variables, one row per sample, and splits the variation into a constrained and an unconstrained part. It is not implemented, and the decision is to leave it for now.

What it would take:

  • The maths fits the long-table approach. Regress the centred table on X through a QR of X: the fitted part has rank at most the number of variables, so its SVD is small, and the residual is the sparse table minus a low-rank part, which the implicit operator used for clr can handle with irlba.
  • Partial RDA (Condition()) has the same structure.
  • The cost is the permutation test. vegan::anova(), permutest(), RsquareAdj() and ordiR2step() read the dense fitted matrix stored in the object, which we do not have. We would write our own test: permuting the samples only needs the small matrix Q'Y recomputed, one sparse product per permutation, so it is feasible but is new code and a new object layout, not a flag on el_rda().

What works now instead:

  • vegan::envfit() fits variables to the axes of an unconstrained el_rda() result or of metaMDS() on an el_vegdist() distance, with permutation p-values (tested, including missing values with na.rm = TRUE). It is a post-hoc fit, not a constrained ordination.
  • vegan::dbrda() and capscale() take the dist from el_vegdist(). The distance matrix grows with the square of the number of samples, which is fine up to a few thousand.
  • vegan::adonis2() on a dist tests variables against the whole community.

Revisit it if constrained ordination of large tables, rather than of the distance matrix, turns out to be needed.

Benchmark machine

Timings and peak memory in this document marked “measured on sequoia” come from one shared server. They are indicative, not a specification: wall times depend on how busy the machine is, and peak memory does not.

CPU AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, 12 cores, 24 hardware threads, one socket
Memory 125 GB RAM
Disk NVMe SSD
System Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.8
Software R 4.6.1, duckplyr 1.2.1, duckdb 1.5.4, vegan 2.7.5
Load Shared with other users’ jobs; load average typically 16–24 on the 24 threads
  • Because the machine is busy, a run with threads = 12 competes for cores and is slower than on an idle machine of the same size. Compare methods measured in the same session rather than across sessions.
  • Peak memory is the resident set size (VmHWM in /proc/self/status) of the R process, which includes the DuckDB engine running inside it. Other users’ jobs do not affect it.
  • The package is installed with R CMD INSTALL and run with Rscript. devtools::load_all() compiles with -O0 and is about ten times slower, so it is not used for timings.
  • bench/gen.R writes a synthetic table as Parquet with a given number of samples, taxa and rows. Taxon frequencies follow a power law (Zipf), so a few taxa occur in nearly every sample. That is the expensive case for the pairwise kernel, whose work grows with the square of the number of samples per taxon. bench/run.R times el_vegdist() on such a file and reports the peak resident memory.
  • The largest tables here (20,000 samples, 499,000 taxa) were run only on this server. A dense matrix of that table would take about 80 GB, which does not fit on a 30 GB laptop; the long-table methods needed 2–4 GB.

Testing against vegan

This is the main deliverable.

  • vegan is in Suggests: the tests use it, and eigenvals() for ecolongr_rda is registered only when it is loaded. The package itself never calls it.
  • Fixtures: vegan::varespec, vegan::dune, and a synthetic sparse community generated with a fixed seed.
  • Compare with testthat at a tolerance of about 1e-10 for distances and transforms.
  • Compare ordinations up to sign: eigenvalues, scores and proportion explained.
  • Corner cases, each a separate test:
    • sample with all zeros, listed in samples: must match vegan on the matrix that includes the zero row
    • the same sample with samples omitted: must match vegan on the matrix without it
    • taxon present in a single sample
    • sample with a single taxon
    • samples with identical profiles
    • binary = TRUE
  • Check that tests can fail: for each, a plausible wrong implementation (for example Bray–Curtis on relative abundances, or PCA without centring) must produce a failing test.
  • Memory benchmark against vegan and mia on synthetic datasets, reporting peak memory and run time: see “Cost” and the README.

Existing packages to check first

Only the CRAN descriptions have been read so far, not the function lists.

  • proxyC: proximity on large sparse matrices in C++. Not yet checked whether it has Bray–Curtis.
  • rbiom: beta diversity, including UniFrac, on BIOM data.
  • irlba, RSpectra: sparse truncated SVD.
  • mia 1.20.0 (Bioconductor), read on 2026-10-19: no sparse path. getDissimilarity() calls vegan::vegdist() on the dense transposed assay, and transformAssay() calls vegan::decostand(). Its PCA is scater::runPCA() on the transformed, dense assay. The README has timings against vegan and mia.

If one of them already computes a measure correctly on sparse input, a thin wrapper plus the vegan comparison tests may be enough for that measure.

Open questions

  • Whether to also accept a sparse matrix directly, or leave the conversion to the user.
  • Whether to also accept tbl_lazy from dbplyr and Arrow datasets. Data frames and duckplyr tables are accepted; no test covers the others.
  • Whether omitting samples should only be documented, or also give a message that all-zero samples cannot be detected.
  • Whether to add rda with explanatory variables (see above).
  • How the cost of the matrix completion grows with ropt above 3 on large tables, which has not been measured.
  • Which of the other vegan::vegdist indices are worth the effort.
  • Richness estimators of the breakaway type are decided against, for now. el_frequency_counts() gives their input, and breakaway reads it after a split by sample and a sort by count (the help page shows the pipeline, in parallel with purrr and mirai). On simulated frequency tables of 500 samples, breakaway 5.0.1 (GitHub; the CRAN 4.8.4 is no longer maintained) took 0.1-0.4 s per sample on one core, all of it in fitting the models, so a reimplementation would not save time on the large table, which is what this package is for. The estimates also depend strongly on the cutoff argument (about 80,000, 9,000 and 8,000 ASVs for the default, 10 and 20 on one sample with 6,271 observed), which speed does not change. breakaway is GPL-2 and its documentation does not state the model-selection criterion or the standard-error formula, so an implementation would have to follow the papers (Willis and Bunge 2015, doi:10.1111/biom.12332) and could not be compared to 1e-10. Tables without singletons (DADA2 output) need breakaway_nof1(). DivNet is out of scope.
